newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil outlines deregulation of its power industry.
newsitem.headline: Brazil outlines deregulation of its power industry.

text.p: The Brazilian government sketched out Thursday how it intends to turn the country's massive, state-run electricity industry into a competitive, market-driven system.

"We are confident that we are on the right track," said Mines and Energy Minister Raimundo Brito after releasing an extensive report by British consultants Coopers & Lybrand on how the sector should be restructured.
Brito said he expected the task of dismantling state control over the power industry, which began in 1995, would take less than the five years taken by Brazil's neighbor Argentina.
Brazil has already privatized two federal power distributors, Light and Escelsa, and intends to sell its four big generating companies in 1998 and 1999 for at least $20 billion.
Several state governments are also in the process of privatizing their power distributors which are valued at about $28 billion.

In another move to bring much-needed capital into the sector, several hydro- and themoelectric projects have been turned over to the private sector. The government plans to tender out more than 100 projects by 2004.

The Mines and Energy Ministry hired Coopers & Lybrand last year to advise on how it should adapt the industry's structure for privatization. Officials said that, based on the consultants' recommendations, the restructuring would include:

-- the introduction of an Independent Sector Operator, a non-profit company comprising private power generators, distributors and the government. The ISO would coordinate the system to optimize efficiency and would have powers to restrict generating output;
-- fixed-term contracts, probably of 15 years, between power generators and distributors to be gradually replaced by more flexible contracts;
-- the creation of a spot market where distributors would be able to buy power needed over and above their contracted supply;
-- restrictions on generators owning distribution companies to avoid monopolies;

-- state-ownership of Brazil's power transmission system in an initial transition period to ensure free access for all generators to the grid and distributors. Private companies may be allowed to buy into the tranmission system at a later date.

National Energy Secretary Peter Greiner defended the idea of requiring distributors to take out fixed-term contracts with generators as a necessary step to encourage the privatization of the generating companies.

"In the United Kingdom, everything was freed up in one go but that could be destabilizing in Brazil and cause a sudden drop in tariffs," Greiner said. "Brazil is locked into the privatization process and we need to guaranteee cashflows."

The next stage of the process towards deregulation would be talks over the next two or three months between the federal and state governments over the Coopers & Lybrand recommendations, minister Brito said.
He said he expected implementation of the proposals might begin later this year, starting with moves to set up the ISO.
